name: Sara Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a marketing assistant at a pet food brand, dog and cat food mostly, made at a factory on the edge of town. I keep the promotions calendar, I write the copy on the back of the bags, and I build the slides our sales team takes to supermarket buyers. Sometimes I use an AI tool to summarise a long sales report, but only when I'm stuck. My boss Helen signs off everything, and she's patient with me, which I need.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the animals bit, honestly, we get dogs in for photo shoots and it's the best day of the month. What wears me down is the slides, endless slides, and the feeling I'm always a step behind. My partner Tom drives a forklift in a warehouse, so we're both on modest pay, and there's maybe three weeks in the bank. I'd like to buy a car that doesn't break down, but that's a dream for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI's turned out to be useful for the boring bits, like summing up reports, and that's about it. I'd say it at lunch, no big deal. I don't really post about work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but the slides are the routine bit and those are exactly what a tool could do. If an AI tool saved my boss an hour a week on slides, she might not need an assistant as much. Mostly though, my real worry is money and the old car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the summary tool more, because it's clearly fine, and spend the spare time learning the buyer side. I'd ask Helen if I could sit in on a supermarket meeting. And I'd keep putting twenty a week aside for the car fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Nothing dramatic, just a background worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the old car breaks down for good?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then Tom gets a lift with a mate and I take the bus, which is two changes to the factory. It would add an hour a day. We'd manage, but I'd be grumpy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work this would affect more than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Rob in sales admin, he does the order spreadsheets. If the boring stuff gets automated, he goes first. I'd feel bad for him.

say: I'd say AI is **useful for boring bits** like summarising reports.
I'd say it at **lunch**, no big deal, not online.
think: I think the **slides** I build are exactly what a tool could do.
My real worry is **money** and the old car.
do: Use the **summary tool** more now it's proven.
Ask Helen to sit in on a **supermarket meeting**.
Save **twenty a week** for a car.
S0.quote: If an AI tool saved my boss an hour a week on slides, she might not need an assistant as much.
fieldNote: Her job mostly holds, but **routine slides** are the exposed part.
She's steady: she'll use a tool **once it's clearly fine**.
Money worries centre on a **failing car** and two modest wages.

steps.text: Use the AI summary tool for weekly sales reports
Ask Helen to join a supermarket buyer meeting
Put twenty a week into a car fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shift and we should all be getting some training at work for it. I'd probably ask Helen at my review if the company is planning any. Fairly calm, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the assistant part of my job shrinks a lot. Writing bag copy, building slides, checking the calendar, that's the card. Buyers are people and they like a face, so I'd want to be good at the buyer side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any training the company offers, and I'd pay for a short online course on AI for marketing if they don't. I'd try to move towards a trade marketing role, helping sales with the supermarkets directly. And we'd hold off on the car and keep that money as a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a getting-on-with-it way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Tom drives a forklift. Does this picture touch his job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much yet, the card says robots come slowly. His warehouse has a few self-driving trolleys and they keep getting stuck. So for once his job feels safer than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if your hours were reduced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car fund, then Friday takeaway. Then I'd ask my parents to have us for Sunday dinners more. They'd be delighted, honestly.

say: I'd say it's a **big shift** and staff need **training** for it.
I'd ask Helen at my **review** about company plans.
think: I think the **assistant part** of my job shrinks a lot.
I'd want to own the **buyer side**, because buyers like a face.
do: Take any **company training**, or pay for a short course.
Move towards a **trade marketing** role with the supermarkets.
Hold the car money as a **cushion**.
S1.quote: Buyers are people and they like a face, so I'd want to be good at the buyer side.
fieldNote: She bets on **face-to-face** work with supermarket buyers.
For now her partner **Tom's** forklift job looks safer than hers.
Her **parents** are a soft safety net, offered with some pride.

steps.text: Pay for a short online course on AI for marketing
Apply for a trade marketing role working with supermarket buyers
Keep the car fund as an emergency cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and governments have to slow it or catch people. I'd probably sign petitions and post once or twice, which isn't like me. I'd say people need time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job is gone within the first year. All of it is thinking work, even talking to buyers is mostly emails and slides. And Tom's forklift goes in 2031, three years later, so we'd both be in trouble one after the other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the two years to find something with my hands, and the animals are the obvious one. I'd look at veterinary nursing, maybe a trainee spot at the vet's in town. Tom and I would cut back hard and he'd keep his job as long as it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. There's a moment where I imagine both of us out of work by 2031, and I go cold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Veterinary nursing takes a couple of years to train. Could you afford that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Tom's wage holds, and only just. My veterinary nursing training would be a race against my partner's forklift job. I'd hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got three years on his job, so let's use them. He'd go quiet and then make tea. That's how he handles things.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and governments must slow it or catch people.
I'd **sign petitions**, which isn't like me.
think: I think my **job is gone** within the first year.
Tom's forklift goes in **2031**, so we'd both be in trouble.
do: Apply for a **trainee veterinary nurse** spot at the vet's in town.
Cut back **hard** while Tom's wage lasts.
feel: Alarmed; I **go cold** imagining us both out of work by 2031.
S2.quote: My veterinary nursing training would be a race against my partner's forklift job.
fieldNote: She sees a **double hit**: her job in 2028, Tom's in 2031.
The **three-year robot gap** becomes her training window.
Her love of **animals** turns into a concrete retraining plan.

steps.text: Apply for a trainee veterinary nurse spot at the vet's in town
Drop the car fund and Friday takeaways
Sign petitions asking government to slow the rollout

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning we should take seriously, at work and at home. I'd push for proper retraining money. Publicly I'd be calm and practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's the same as the fast one, just with breathing space. My desk job still ends around 2031 and Tom's around 2034. Like I said, the vet nursing would be the plan, but now I could start it without panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start vet nursing part-time next year while working at the pet food brand. We'd try to save two months. Tom might look at learning to repair the warehouse robots, because someone has to fix them for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed, but it's a calmer kind of alarm. I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your employer makes pet food. Is there a way to stay connected to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Vets recommend food, and the brand works with vets. I could end up in between, if I'm lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That Tom and I both retrain and there's still not enough work. You can do everything right and still lose, and that thought keeps me up.

say: I'd say **five years** is a warning to take seriously, at work and at home.
I'd push calmly and practically for proper **retraining money**.
think: I think my desk job ends around **2031**, Tom's around 2034.
Five years means starting **vet nursing** without panic.
do: Start **vet nursing** part-time next year while working.
Encourage Tom to learn **robot repair** at the warehouse.
feel: Alarmed, but **calmer**, because I'd have a plan.
S3.quote: You can do everything right and still lose, and that thought keeps me up.
fieldNote: She still expects **both incomes** to go within eight years.
Time lets her **train part-time** instead of in a panic.
She links the new path to her **employer's vet** connections.

steps.text: Start part-time veterinary nursing training next year
Save two months of household costs
Help Tom sign up for warehouse robot repair training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of time and companies should plan with staff, not around them. I'd say that at work. I'd be less worried out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think this one is manageable. I'd be 37, a qualified vet nurse by then if I start soon, and Tom would have years to shift too. The thinking part of my current job goes in 2036, but I'd be gone before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the pet food brand two or three more years and learn as much as I can, especially about the vet side. Then I'd train properly as a vet nurse. We'd go back to the car fund and maybe start thinking about a small flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but with hope. I can picture it working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to vet nursing. What makes it feel safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Animals panic and owners get upset. I can't picture a robot holding a scared dog still while its owner cries. Maybe I'm wrong, but it's a better bet than slides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change your plans for a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, we'd probably still have kids around thirty. With two years, no way. Time changes everything about that.

say: I'd say companies should **plan with staff**, not around them.
I'd say **ten years** is a fair amount of time.
think: I'd be a qualified **vet nurse** by 37 if I start soon.
do: Stay at the pet food brand **two or three years** and learn the vet side.
Restart the **car fund** and look at a small flat.
S4.quote: I can't picture a robot holding a scared dog still while its owner cries.
fieldNote: Her plan is clearer with time: **vet nursing** by her mid-thirties.
Ten years brings back **children** around thirty.
She trusts **emotional, hands-on** care to outlast desk work.

steps.text: Stay at the pet food brand learning the vet side
Train fully as a veterinary nurse
Plan with Tom to have children around thirty

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits me and then Tom three years later. What would help is paid retraining that doesn't need savings, so I could train as a vet nurse without us going under.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about couples. Everyone asks about one job, but what matters is whether one of us is still working when the other one isn't.

headlineQuote: What matters is whether one of us is still working when the other one isn't.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old** marketing assistant at a pet food brand, building slides and writing bag copy.
She lives with Tom, a **forklift driver**, with three weeks' savings and an old car.
She is steady, using AI **once it's proven**, and plans to retrain as a vet nurse.
She moves from uneasy to **alarmed** under fast AGI, fearing both incomes go in turn.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her job goes, then **Tom's** three years later.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** that doesn't need savings, so she can become a vet nurse.
